<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj:switching_n_main_eigenvalues}
For any unsigned connected graph $G \notin\{ K_2, K_4 - e\}$, there is a switching $\mbox{\boldmath $s$}$ such that all (distinct) eigenvalues of $G^{\mbox{\boldmath $s$}}$ are main.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- conjecture-2: body_md -->
\label{conj:switching_n_main_eigenvectors}
For any unsigned connected graph $G \notin\{ K_2, K_4 - e\}$ of order $n$, there is a  switching $\mbox{\boldmath $s$}$ such that $G^{\mbox{\boldmath $s$}}$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis consisting of main eigenvectors.
<!-- end conjecture-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:equivalence}
Conjectures \ref{conj:switching_n_main_eigenvalues} and \ref{conj:switching_n_main_eigenvectors} are equivalent.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We only need to argue that Conjecture \ref{conj:switching_n_main_eigenvalues} implies Conjecture \ref{conj:switching_n_main_eigenvectors}; the other direction is clear. 

Assume that there is a switching $\mbox{\boldmath $s$}$ such that all distinct eigenvalues of $G^{\mbox{\boldmath $s$}}$ are main. Since $A(G^{\mbox{\boldmath $s$}})$ is symmetric, the eigenspaces corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. So it suffices to find an orthogonal basis of main eigenvectors for $E_{\lambda}$ for any given eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $G^{\mbox{\boldmath $s$}}$.

Let $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}_1$ denote the normalized orthogonal projection of $\1$ on $E_{\lambda}$. Since $E_{\lambda}\not \subseteq \1^\perp$, we have $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}_1 \ne \0$. Extend $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}_1$ to an orthonormal basis $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}_1, \ldots, \mbox{\boldmath $x$}_{m_{\lambda}}$ of $E_{\lambda}$ where $m_{\lambda}=\dim E_\lambda$. Clearly, $\1^\top \mbox{\boldmath $x$}_i = 0$ for all $2\le i\le m_\lambda$. Now, take an $m_\lambda\times m_\lambda$ orthogonal matrix $Q$ whose first row is
\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{m_\lambda}}(1, \ldots, 1).\]
Such a matrix exists by extending the above row to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^{m_\lambda}$. Define 
\[ \mbox{\boldmath $y$}_{j} = \sum_{i=1}^{m_\lambda} Q_{ij} \mbox{\boldmath $x$}_{i}.\]
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, $\mbox{\boldmath $y$}_1, \ldots, \mbox{\boldmath $y$}_{m_\lambda}$ form an orthonormal basis for $E_{\lambda}$. Moreover, we see that
\[ \1^\top \mbox{\boldmath $y$}_j = Q_{1j} \1^\top \mbox{\boldmath $x$}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{m_\lambda}}\1^\top \mbox{\boldmath $x$}_1 \neq 0. \]
Thus, $\mbox{\boldmath $y$}_1, \ldots, \mbox{\boldmath $y$}_{m_\lambda}$ are main eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda$ for $G^{\mbox{\boldmath $s$}}$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:asymptotic}
Let $G$ be a graph of order $n$.  Then there exists a switching
$\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\in\{\pm1\}^n$ such that
\[
M(\mbox{\boldmath $s$})\ge  n - O\!\left(\frac{n}{(\log n)^{1/4}}\right)= n(1-o(1)).
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:asymptotic_distinct}
Let $G$ be a graph with $d\ge 2$ distinct eigenvalues. Then there exists a switching
$\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\in\{\pm1\}^n$ such that
\[
M_*(\mbox{\boldmath $s$})\ge  d - O\!\left(\frac{d}{(\log d)^{1/4}}\right).
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
Show that the switching conjecture for main eigenvalues holds for trees and connected regular graphs of order $n\ge 3$.
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- conjecture-3: body_md -->
\label{conj:signature}
For any unsigned connected graph $G$ of order $n\ge 3$, there exists a signature $\sigma$ such that all eigenvalues of the signed graph $(G,\sigma)$ are main.
<!-- end conjecture-3 -->
<!-- conjecture-4: body_md -->
Fix a Rademacher vector $\mbox{\boldmath $b$}\in \{\pm 1\}^n$. For any unsigned connected graph $G \notin\{ K_2, K_4 - e\}$ of order $n$, there is a  switching $\mbox{\boldmath $s$}$ such that $G^{\mbox{\boldmath $s$}}$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis consisting of eigenvectors which are all non-orthogonal to $\mbox{\boldmath $b$}$.
<!-- end conjecture-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:Littlewood_Offord}
If $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ has at least $\ell$ nonzero coordinates, and $\mbox{\boldmath $s$}$ is a random switching, then
\[
        \mathbb{P}(\mbox{\boldmath $s$}^\top \mbox{\boldmath $x$}=0)
        \le
        2^{-\ell}\binom{\ell}{\lfloor \frac{\ell}{2}\rfloor}. 
\]
Equivalently, the number of Rademacher vectors $\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\in \{\pm 1\}^n$ orthogonal to $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}$ is at most $2^{n-\ell}\binom{\ell}{\lfloor \frac{\ell}{2}\rfloor}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
\label{claim:large_support} We have 
\[\sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda_L^c} m_\lambda \mathbb{P}(\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\perp E_\lambda)\le n\, O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\right).\]
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
If $\lambda\in \Lambda_L^c$, it means that every (non-zero) eigenvector $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}\in E_\lambda$ has $|\operatorname{supp}(\mbox{\boldmath $x$})|\ge L+1$. Pick a $\lambda$-eigenvector $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}$. Using Theorem \ref{thm:Littlewood_Offord}, we see that 
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda_L^c} m_\lambda \mathbb{P}(\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\perp E_\lambda)& \le \sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda_L^c} m_\lambda \mathbb{P}(\mbox{\boldmath $s$}^\top \mbox{\boldmath $x$} = 0)\\
        & \le \left(\sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda_L^c} m_\lambda\right) 2^{-(L+1)}\binom{L+1}{\lfloor \frac{L+1}{2}\rfloor} \\
        & = n \, O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\right),
    \end{align*}
    where the last inequality follows from Stirling's approximation.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- claim-2: body_md -->
\label{claim:small_support} We have
    \[\sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda_L} m_\lambda \mathbb{P}(\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\perp E_\lambda)\le L^2\, 2^{L\choose 2}. \]
<!-- end claim-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Consider a (non-zero) eigenvector $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}\in E_\lambda$ with minimum support. Since $\lambda \in \Lambda_L$, we see that $|\operatorname{supp}(\mbox{\boldmath $x$})|\le L$. It is clear that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the induced subgraph $G[\operatorname{supp}(\mbox{\boldmath $x$})]$ with eigenvector $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}|_{\operatorname{supp}(\mbox{\boldmath $x$})}$ (restriction of $\mbox{\boldmath $x$}$ to $\operatorname{supp}(\mbox{\boldmath $x$})$). In particular, this means that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of some graph on at most $L$ vertices. We see that $|\Lambda_L|\le |\mathcal{E}(L)|$, where 
    \[\mathcal{E}(L):=\{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}: \lambda \text{ is an eigenvalue of some graph on at most $L$ vertices} \}.\] 

    Furthermore, it is well-known that a space of dimension $k$ contains at most $2^k$ Rademacher vectors. Thus, the number of Rademacher vectors in the space $E_{\lambda}^\perp$ is at most $2^{n-m_\lambda}$. This implies
    \[ \mathbb{P}(\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\perp E_\lambda)
        \le
        2^{-m_\lambda}.\]
    Using the above observations, we conclude that 
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda_L} m_\lambda \mathbb{P}(\mbox{\boldmath $s$}\perp E_\lambda) & \le  \sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda_L} m_\lambda\, 2^{-m_\lambda}\\
        & \le \frac{1}{2}|\Lambda_L|\\
        & \le \frac{1}{2}|\mathcal{E}(L)|\\
        & < \sum_{k=1}^L k\,2^{k\choose 2}\\
        & \le L^2\, 2^{L\choose 2}. 
    \end{align*}
The second last inequality above holds because there are at most $2^{k\choose 2}$ labelled graphs on $k$ vertices, each of which can have at most $k$ distinct eigenvalues. This completes the proof of the claim.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
